beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: This jug has water in it, and a scale up its side. How many liters of water are in the jug?

do.text: How many liters of water are in the jug?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: The water is almost at the ten. Ten liters!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Or the five, just below? But the water sits between them, on a mark with no number at all.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: When marks have no numbers, one question unlocks the scale. What is one mark worth?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: How do we find out?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Watch. We peel the scale off the jug, and lay it flat. Every measuring tool is a number line, standing up.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Zero, five, and ten are printed. The rest are only marks.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Count the spaces from zero to five. One, two, three, four, five.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Five liters in five equal spaces. Five divided by five is one. So each mark is worth one liter.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now read the water. Start at five, and hop up by ones. Six, seven, eight.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Eight liters! Not ten, and not five.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now stand the line back up on the jug. The top of the water meets the eight. Same line, same reading.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A new jug, the same question. The water is between twenty and thirty.

do.text: How many liters of water are in the jug?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: First, what is one mark worth?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Peel it off, and lay it flat. Count the spaces from zero to ten. One, two, three, four, five.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Ten liters in five spaces. Ten divided by five is two. Each mark is worth two liters, not one.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: So I count by twos. Twenty two, twenty four. Twenty four liters!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Stand it back up, and the water meets twenty four. Different marks, same method.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A quick feel for the units. Liters tell us how much liquid. Grams and kilograms tell us how heavy.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A big bottle of water holds about one liter, and weighs about one kilogram.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: And a gram?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A paper clip weighs about one gram. A thousand of them make a kilogram.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: When a balance is level, both sides weigh exactly the same.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A bag and a weight of two hundred fifty grams on the left. One kilogram on the right. How heavy is the bag?

do.text: The balance is level. What is the mass of the bag, in grams?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: One kilogram is a thousand grams!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: So the bag and the weight make a thousand. Let us draw that as one long bar.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Take away the two hundred fifty, and what is left is the bag. A thousand minus two hundred fifty.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Seven hundred fifty grams!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A thermometer is a number line standing up. What is one mark worth? From ten to twenty there are five spaces. Ten divided by five is two.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: So each mark is two degrees. From twenty, I count twenty two, twenty four. Twenty four degrees!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Two thermometers? Read each, then subtract. If the morning was twelve, the afternoon is twelve degrees warmer.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Once we can read the numbers, stories in one unit are ordinary arithmetic. Add, subtract, multiply or divide.

do.text: Same unit: just do the arithmetic

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A bucket holds nine liters, and a tub holds three. How many together? Hop nine, then hop three.

do.text: A bucket holds 9 liters of water and a tub holds 3 liters. How many liters do they hold together?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Twelve liters!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Next, twenty four liters of juice go into jugs that hold four liters each. How many jugs?

do.text: 24 liters of juice are poured equally into jugs of 4 liters. How many jugs?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Hop by four. Four, eight, twelve, sixteen, twenty, twenty four.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Six hops, so six jugs!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Five bags of rice, three kilograms each. Three, six, nine, twelve, fifteen.

do.text: Each bag of rice has a mass of 3 kilograms. What is the mass of 5 bags, in kilograms?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Five threes. Fifteen kilograms!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A jug, a balance, a thermometer. The jug and the thermometer each hide a number line.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The jug's scale lies down, zero to ten. One mark is one liter, and the water reads eight.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The balance is level, so the bag is seven hundred fifty grams: two hundred fifty more makes a thousand.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The thermometer: marks worth two degrees, and the liquid reads twenty four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: For the jug and the thermometer, find what one mark is worth, then read it like a number line.

do.text: 2. Read it like a number line.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A balance has no marks. When it is level, both sides weigh the same.
